scenes.heading: The immune system
scenes.sub: You meet millions of microbes a day. Why aren't you always sick?
scenes.say: Every day your body meets millions of microorganisms, yet you're only sick now and then. That's thanks to your immune system. It keeps pathogens out, attacks any that get in, and remembers them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Festival fence, roaming guards, then police hunting one face
scenes.science: Barriers, non-specific defences, then specific lymphocytes
scenes.breaks: festival security works one layer after another, but the body's lines overlap and talk to each other, and they never close.
scenes.say: Think of security at a music festival. The fence and gates stop most people sneaking in. Guards roam the crowd removing any troublemaker. And the police hunt for one particular wanted face. Those are your three lines of defence.

scenes.heading: First line: barriers
points: Cilia sweep mucus away from the lungs
Lysozyme in tears breaks bacterial walls
scenes.say: The first line is barriers. Skin is tough and waterproof. Sticky mucus traps pathogens, and cilia sweep it away from the lungs. Stomach acid kills pathogens in food, and tears contain lysozyme, which breaks down bacterial cell walls.

scenes.heading: Second line: non-specific
scenes.say: If pathogens get in, the second line attacks any invader. Phagocytes are like Pac-Man: they engulf pathogens and digest them. Inflammation widens nearby blood vessels and makes them leakier, bringing more white blood cells. That causes redness, heat, swelling and pain.

scenes.heading: Antigens vs antibodies

right.title: Antibody
points: Y-shaped protein made by B cells
Fits one antigen: lock and key

scenes.say: The third line is specific. Antigens are molecules on the pathogen. Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells, and each fits one antigen, like a lock and key. They clump pathogens, block viruses and neutralise toxins. T cells help and destroy infected cells.

scenes.heading: Antibody graph
scenes.question: First infection: antibodies take about a week to rise to a low peak. Second time: they rise within days, much higher. Why?
lines: First time: few B cells match
They take time to divide: slow, small
Second time: memory cells act fast
scenes.say: The first time you meet a virus, only a few B cells match, so antibodies take about a week to rise and the peak is low. But memory cells were made. Next time, they recognise the antigen fast, so antibodies rise within days, much higher. That's immunity.

scenes.heading: Why colds come back
points: Antibodies are specific to one antigen
scenes.say: So why do you keep catching colds? Immunity is specific. Many different viruses cause colds, and viruses like influenza change their antigens, so your memory cells may not recognise them.

points: First line: skin, mucus, cilia, acid
Third line: B cells and T cells
Memory cells give a faster response
scenes.say: Quick recap. Barriers come first, then phagocytes and inflammation, then specific B and T cells. Memory cells give a faster, stronger response next time. Now try the practice questions!
